summary: Defines the information model used by IPFIX for encoding measured traffic information and details about the observation point, metering and exporting processes. It is open enough to be used by other protocols. It was replaced by RFC 7012.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the dictionary of words, like packet count and source address, that flow reports can use. It was replaced by RFC 7012.

questions: what is the ipfix information model
subtitle: The shared dictionary of named fields that IPFIX flow reports can carry, from source addresses to packet counts.

tldr.problem: The IPFIX protocol defines how data is transmitted, but not which flow attributes (such as source IP address or number of packets) and which details about the metering and exporting processes can be sent.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5102 defines a template for describing each Information Element, a type space of abstract data types, an IANA-managed identifier range of 1-32767, and a list of Information Elements grouped into 12 categories.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5102 was obsoleted by RFC 7012 and updated by RFC 6313, so it is a historical definition of the IPFIX information model rather than the current one.

today: RFC 5102 has been obsoleted by RFC 7012, which is now the definition of the IPFIX information model, and it was also updated by RFC 6313. It remains the original Proposed Standard list of Information Elements from January 2008.

sections.title: Why an Information Model
sections.content:
The IP Flow Information eXport (IPFIX) protocol transmits information about measured IP traffic. The protocol specification in RFC 5101 says how Information Elements are encoded, but it does not list which ones exist. Examples of what could be reported are flow attributes such as the source IP address and the number of packets, or details of the metering process such as the sampling rate and flow timeout interval.

This document fills that gap with the IPFIX information model. The RFC admits that the term is not fully in line with RFC 3444: the model does not specify relationships between Information Elements, and it does not fix a concrete encoding. Other encodings, such as XML-based ones, can be applied.

Much of the text was generated from XML documents. The XML source for the element list and the XML schema for the template and data types are attached as Appendices A and B. The main body is normative and the appendices are informational.
sections.plainLanguage: A club agrees how to send reports, but forgot to write down the list of things you can report. This document is that list.

sections.title: How an Information Element Is Described
sections.content:
Every Information Element, now or in a future extension, MUST have a name, an elementId, a description, a dataType and a status. The status is one of current, deprecated or obsolete. The elementId is globally unique when used without an enterprise identifier, and IANA administers its values.

Enterprise-specific elements MUST also carry an enterpriseId, which makes the identifier globally unique. Valid values are SMI network management private enterprise codes defined by IANA. Optional properties are dataTypeSemantics, units, range and reference.

Elements also have a default scope. Those in Sections 5.2 and 5.3 default to a specific Metering Process or Exporting Process. Those in Sections 5.4 to 5.11 default to a specific Flow. Option Templates can narrow the scope further.
sections.plainLanguage: Each word in the dictionary comes with a card: its name, a number, what it means and what kind of value it holds.

sections.title: Naming Conventions and the post Prefix
sections.content:
Names should be descriptive and start with a lower-case letter. Composed names capitalize the first letter of each later component, and acronyms stay lower-case except for ones such as IPv4 and IPv6. Examples are sourceMacAddress and destinationIPv4Address. Names of elements that are not enterprise-specific MUST be unique within the model, and enterprise-specific ones SHOULD be prefixed with a vendor name.

A name prefix of post marks a property measured after a middlebox may have changed it. The Observation Point sees the packet before the middlebox, but the post value is obtained within the Observation Domain by other means that are considered sufficiently reliable, for example by analyzing a packet marker's marking tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Names are written like sourceMacAddress. A name starting with post means 'what it looked like after something changed it on the way'.

sections.title: The Type Space
sections.content:
Section 3 defines the abstract data types an element can use. There are eight integer types (unsigned8 up to unsigned64, and signed8 up to signed64), float32 and float64 (IEEE 754), boolean, macAddress (a string of 6 octets), octetArray, string (Unicode), ipv4Address and ipv6Address. There are also four time types based on UTC: dateTimeSeconds, dateTimeMilliseconds, dateTimeMicroseconds and dateTimeNanoseconds. Leap seconds are excluded, and the epoch is left to the encoding specification.

Integral types can carry data type semantics. A quantity is a discrete measured value and is the default. A totalCounter keeps counting independently of export. A deltaCounter is reset to 0 each time its value is exported. Both wrap to zero at the limit of the type. An identifier supports only equality checks, and flags is a set of bit fields that should always be unsigned.
sections.plainLanguage: Each value has a kind: a whole number, a piece of text, a time, or an address. Counters are like odometers, and a delta counter goes back to zero each time you read it out.

sections.title: Element Identifiers
sections.content:
IANA assigns the identifier of every element. Values are in the range 1-32767, and 0 is reserved. The sub-range 1-127 is compatible with the field types of NetFlow version 9 (RFC 3954), and 128-32767 holds further elements. Section 4 of the RFC lists all elements by number.

Enterprise-specific elements use the same 1-32767 range, but the identifier is coupled with an enterprise identifier, so two enterprises can reuse the same number for different purposes and a Collecting Process can still tell them apart. Enterprise identifiers MUST be registered as SMI private enterprise code numbers with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: Every word in the dictionary gets a number, handed out by one office so no two words share one. Companies can add their own words by also stamping their company number.

sections.title: The Twelve Groups of Information Elements
sections.content:
Section 5, the main part of the document, groups the elements into 12 categories: identifiers; metering and exporting process configuration; metering and exporting process statistics; IP header fields; transport header fields; sub-IP header fields; derived packet properties; min/max flow properties; flow timestamps; per-flow counters; miscellaneous flow properties; and padding.

Elements derived from packet fields or packet treatment (groups 4 to 7) can typically serve as Flow Keys. If such a value changes from packet to packet within a Flow, the model says it is determined by the first packet observed, unless the element says otherwise. Only properties that depend on more than one packet, such as those in groups 8 to 11, need updating for later packets.

Examples are the flowKeyIndicator element, a 64-bit set of flags marking which fields of a Data Record are Flow Keys, and tcpControlBits, which records a bit as 1 if any observed packet in the Flow had that TCP control bit set. The identifiers group includes observationDomainId, where a value of 0 means no specific Observation Domain is identified, and templateId, where Template IDs of Data Sets are numbered from 256 to 65535.
sections.plainLanguage: The dictionary is sorted into 12 chapters, like 'who are you', 'what do your packets look like', 'when did it start' and 'how much was sent'.

sections.title: Timestamps, Counters and Flow Endings
sections.content:
Timestamps such as flowStartSeconds and flowEndMilliseconds are absolute. flowStartDeltaMicroseconds and flowEndDeltaMicroseconds are negative offsets from the export time in the IPFIX Message Header, valid only within one message, and the largest offset they can encode is 1 hour, 11 minutes, and 34.967295 seconds. flowStartSysUpTime and flowEndSysUpTime are relative to the last (re-)initialization of the device.

Per-flow counters cannot be part of a Flow Key. They can be running counters or delta counters. For example, octetDeltaCount is the number of octets since the previous report, including IP header and payload, and the post variants report values after a middlebox function. There are also counters per TCP flag, such as tcpSynTotalCount.

The flowEndReason element tells why a Flow was terminated: idle timeout, active timeout, end of Flow detected (for example a TCP FIN), forced end, or lack of resources. flowDirection has only two defined values, 0x00 for ingress and 0x01 for egress. The single padding element paddingOctets lets implementations align data to 4-octet or 8-octet boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Reports say when a conversation started and ended, how much was sent, and why the report was closed, such as 'nobody talked for a while'.

sections.title: Extending the Model
sections.content:
A key requirement for IPFIX is that the set of reported elements can grow. Each new element MUST get a unique identifier, and using IETF and IANA mechanisms is RECOMMENDED for generally applicable elements. New names SHOULD follow the naming conventions, and new abstract data types MUST be defined in IETF Standards Track documents.

Enterprises may define their own elements without registering them with IANA, but they should first consider whether the element is generally applicable. IPFIX does not support enterprise-specific abstract data types.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add new words to the dictionary. Everyone can ask for a shared word, and a company can invent a private one, but nobody can invent new kinds of values.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA created a registry of IPFIX Information Element identifiers with the initial list from Section 4. New assignments go through Expert Review, and requests that duplicate existing functionality SHOULD be declined. The smallest available identifier SHOULD be assigned, and new specifications MUST use the template from Section 2.1.

A second registry holds MPLS label types for element 46, mplsTopLabelType, with 5 types initially defined. The RFC also registers an XML namespace and an XML schema URN, both ending in ipfix-info-15.
sections.plainLanguage: An office keeps the official list. To add a word you ask the office, and they say no if you only want a copy of a word that already exists.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The model does not itself introduce security issues, but it defines attributes that can be sensitive for privacy or business reasons. Exporting header field values may make attacks possible for the receiver that would otherwise be possible only for direct observers of the flows.

The underlying protocol must therefore guarantee the integrity and confidentiality of exported information; this is handled in the IPFIX protocol document, RFC 5101. No element carries keying material, and if future extensions add one, appropriate precautions are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic reports can reveal private things, so the thing carrying them has to lock them up. This dictionary only names the words.

items.label: active timeout
items.desc: Terminated for reporting while still active.

items.label: end of Flow detected
items.desc: The Metering Process saw end signals such as the TCP FIN flag.

items.label: forced end
items.desc: An external event ended it, such as a shutdown of the Metering Process.

items.label: lack of resources
items.desc: The Metering or Exporting Process ran short of resources.
